1009.title: The Kindertransport
1009.hook: Jewish children are sent to Britain by train and ship, without their parents
1009.howItsDone: Survivors of the Kindertransport and their families have gathered and recorded their stories, and Jewish communities and schools remember the rescue alongside the parents who stayed behind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kristallnacht, and your line: the night of glass. Did a candle or a lit window bring it back to you? Today, what parents did in the months after that night. Go gently. Day one thousand nine.

A railway platform, crowded and strangely quiet. A small girl wears her good coat. Around her neck hangs a cardboard tag with a number on it. She holds one small suitcase, packed by her mother the night before: a few clothes, a photograph, maybe a book. Her parents are kissing her goodbye. They are not getting on the train. Only she is. The whistle blows. Today's word is the name of that train, and of all the trains like it.
screen: `A TAG WITH A NUMBER.` → `ONE SMALL SUITCASE.` → `THE PARENTS STAY BEHIND.`

segments.voice: Kindertransport is German for children's transport. After Kristallnacht, Britain agreed to take in Jewish children from Germany, Austria and nearby lands. Not their parents. Just the children. Jewish groups, Quakers and other volunteers raced to arrange it: lists, papers, families or hostels on the other side, people willing to promise each child's keep. The children went by train to the coast, then by ship across the sea. They were met by strangers. Some were taken into loving homes. Some were moved from place to place. Some were the only Jewish child in a village. When the war began, the way out all but closed, and the rescue nearly ended. For some of the children, that platform was the last time they saw their parents. There is an old story in the Torah about a mother who does the same impossible thing. In Egypt, Pharaoh orders the Hebrew baby boys killed. Moses' mother hides him as long as she can. Then she makes a little ark of reeds, lays him in it, and sets it among the reeds at the river's edge. She lets go of her child to save him. And the Torah adds one line about his older sister: "And his sister stood afar off, to know what would be done to him." Someone watched. Someone wanted to know where he went. Today's word holds two things at once, and neither cancels the other. It was a rescue. Children lived who might not have. And it was a goodbye. Every child on those trains was someone's whole world, handed to strangers by parents who stayed behind.
screen: `CHILDREN'S TRANSPORT.` · `TRAIN, SHIP, A HOME OF STRANGERS.` · `A BASKET IN THE REEDS.` · `A RESCUE AND A GOODBYE.` · then, large: `HIS SISTER STOOD AFAR OFF.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: think of those children. Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Bring to mind one child on that platform, with a tag and a small suitcase. You don't need a name or a face. Just let them be there. Then bring to mind the parents, standing still while the train pulls out. Breathe with both of them. If it's too heavy, let your attention rest on your own breath for a while, and come back when you're ready. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer. If you don't, just keep them company until the bell. The bell holds the time.
The Kindertransport. German for children's transport: the rescue that brought Jewish children to Britain, without their parents, in the months before the war. Today's word.
Your line: the children went alone. Today, when you see a child with a parent, at a bus stop or a school gate, let it remind you of those platforms. Day one thousand nine.

fork.reveal: parents put their children on the trains and stayed behind. like Moses' mother at the river, they let go of their child to save them.

what a scholar hears: a rescue and a separation at once. children lived, and parents stayed behind, some never to see them again.

1010.title: Closed doors
1010.hook: at a conference by a lake, nations refuse refugees; a ship full of Jewish families is turned away
1010.howItsDone: Jewish teaching returns often to the command to love the stranger, and some Jewish refugee organizations today point to this history when they help refugees from anywhere.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kindertransport, and your line: the children went alone. Did a child at a school gate or a bus stop bring those platforms back? Today, the doors that didn't open, for the parents and for so many others. Day one thousand ten.

Where do you go when nobody will let you in? A grand hotel on the shore of a lake in France. Delegates from many countries arrive in good suits. There are speeches, dinners, walks by the water. They have come to talk about Jews trying to get out of Germany and Austria. Delegate after delegate stands up, expresses sympathy, and explains why their own country cannot take more. The meeting ends. The visas don't come. Today's word is what people trying to escape kept finding.
screen: `A HOTEL BY A LAKE.` → `SPEECH AFTER SPEECH OF SYMPATHY.` → `NO VISAS.`

segments.voice: The town was Evian, and the year was 1938. The conference there is remembered for what it did not do. Countries spoke of quotas, of jobs, of their own troubles at home. Very few doors opened. For Jews in Germany and Austria, the problem was no longer only getting out. It was finding anywhere that would let them in. The next year, a ship called the St. Louis sailed from Germany carrying Jewish refugees, families who had sold what they could to buy passage and landing papers for Cuba. When the ship reached Havana, the papers were declared no good, and most of the passengers were not allowed to land. The ship sailed on, close enough to the coast of the United States to see it, and asked to be let in there. The answer was no. Canada said no too. The St. Louis turned around and sailed back across the ocean. In the end, several European countries took the passengers in. Some of them were later caught when the war reached those countries, and did not survive. Closed doors were not only walls and guards. They were forms, quotas, and polite refusals in good suits. The Torah has a command that speaks to it. "Love ye therefore the stranger; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The command rests on memory: you know what it is to be the one outside. Jewish tradition keeps returning to the stranger, the person at the door with nowhere else to go. This chapter is part of why.
screen: `EVIAN: SYMPATHY, BUT NO VISAS.` · `THE ST. LOUIS AT HAVANA.` · `TURNED AWAY, SAILING BACK.` · `REFUSALS IN GOOD SUITS.` · then, large: `LOVE YE THEREFORE THE STRANGER.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: open one door for someone. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind someone who is on the outside of something right now. A newcomer at work. A neighbor who doesn't know anyone. Someone looking for a job, a room, a seat at the table. Stay with them for a moment, without fixing anything. Then let one small opening take shape: an introduction, an invitation, a reference, a chair pulled out. Something you could actually do. Hold it until the bell, and if you can, open it today. The bell holds the time.
Closed doors. The refusals at Evian, the ship turned away from Havana and from North America: the countries that would not let Jewish refugees in. Today's word.
Your line: doors closed. Today, when it is in your power to let someone in, to a conversation, a group, a line, let them in. Day one thousand ten.

what a scholar hears: refusal by paper, quotas and polite speeches, set against a Torah that grounds love of the stranger in memory.

1011.title: The ghettos
1011.hook: Jews are forced into walled, crowded, starving districts of occupied cities
1011.howItsDone: Jews say a blessing before eating, over bread thanking God for bringing bread out of the earth, and some families remember the ghettos at Holocaust memorial gatherings with readings of diaries and testimonies written there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, closed doors, and your line: doors closed. Did you let someone in somewhere, even a small somewhere? Today, the war has begun, and for the Jews of occupied Poland there is no door out at all. Go gently. Day one thousand eleven.

A notice is pasted on a wall in a city in occupied Poland. All Jews must move, by a set date, into a few named streets. Families load carts with whatever they can push: a table, bedding, a sewing machine, the good dishes. Behind them they leave homes they have lived in for years. Ahead of them, workers are building a wall. When it's finished, there will be guards at the gates, and the streets inside will hold far more people than they were ever built for. Today's word is the name for those walled streets.
screen: `A NOTICE ON THE WALL.` → `CARTS FULL OF WHAT THEY COULD CARRY.` → `A WALL GOING UP.`

segments.voice: After the German army occupied Poland and other lands to the east, Jews in city after city were forced into ghettos: sealed districts, closed off by walls or wire, in places like Warsaw and Lodz. Several families shared a single room. Jews had to wear a badge or an armband. Food was rationed on purpose, far below what a body needs. Hunger came first, then disease, and people began to die in the streets. And still, inside the walls, people organized life. House committees ran soup kitchens. Doctors treated the sick with almost nothing. Teachers held classes. Some children squeezed through gaps in the wall to smuggle food back to their families, risking their lives for a few potatoes. Many ghettos had a Jewish council, forced by the Germans to carry out their orders, and people argued then, and historians still argue, about the impossible choices those councils faced. People inside could not know that the ghettos were a stage on the way to something worse. The Torah has a line about hunger, spoken by Moses as he recalls the manna in the wilderness. "Man doth not live by bread only." It does not say bread doesn't matter. In the wilderness, God gave bread. It says a person needs bread and something more. In the ghettos people starved for bread, and they also starved for dignity, for learning, for each other, and they kept feeding that second hunger even when the first could not be fed. Jews bless God before eating bread, thanking God for bringing bread out of the earth. In the ghetto, some said that blessing over almost nothing.
screen: `SEALED DISTRICTS, WALLS AND WIRE.` · `HUNGER, THEN DISEASE.` · `SOUP KITCHENS, CLASSES, SMUGGLERS.` · `BREAD, AND SOMETHING MORE.` · then, large: `MAN DOTH NOT LIVE BY BREAD ONLY.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: pause before your next meal. For now, sit and let your breath slow. Bring to mind the next thing you'll eat. See it plainly: the plate, the bread, the bowl. Let yourself notice what it took to reach you, and how easily it will. Then let the people of the ghettos come to mind, without forcing any picture. Just let them be near. When you do sit down to eat today, stop for one breath before the first bite. If you pray, you can say the blessing your tradition uses before eating. If you don't, the breath is enough. The bell holds the time.
The ghettos. The sealed, crowded, starving districts where Jews in occupied cities were forced to live, and where they still ran soup kitchens and schools. Today's word.
Your line: the ghettos. Today, before you eat, take one breath first, and let it be for the people who had almost nothing to bless. Day one thousand eleven.

1012.title: They wrote it down
1012.hook: Emanuel Ringelblum's team buries the Warsaw ghetto's records in metal boxes and milk cans
1012.howItsDone: The Oneg Shabbat archive is kept and studied today, and Jewish communities read from ghetto diaries and testimonies at Holocaust memorial gatherings so the record is heard aloud.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ghettos, and your line, the same words. Did you stop for one breath before you ate? Today we stay inside the walls of one ghetto, Warsaw, with a group of people who would not let it be forgotten. Day one thousand twelve.

Rubble in a ruined city, some years after the war. A crew is digging under what's left of a building, following directions from someone who survived. A shovel strikes metal. They lift out a battered box, packed tight with paper. Later, nearby, they find milk cans, sealed shut and buried in the same way. Inside: diaries, reports, posters, children's essays, ration cards, a theater ticket. The voice of a whole community, folded into tins. Today's word is what the people who buried them did.
screen: `A SHOVEL STRIKES METAL.` → `MILK CANS FULL OF PAPER.` → `A COMMUNITY FOLDED INTO TINS.`

segments.voice: Emanuel Ringelblum was a historian. When the Warsaw ghetto was sealed, he did what a historian does. He gathered a secret team of writers, teachers, rabbis, economists and young volunteers, and they began to collect everything. They gave their group a code name, Oneg Shabbat, Hebrew for the joy of the Sabbath, because they met on Saturdays. It sounded like a gathering to sing. It was an archive. They wrote reports on hunger and smuggling and how people were dying. They asked people to write about their lives, and children to write about theirs. They kept the German orders, the theater tickets, the soup kitchen menus, the scraps. When the deportations began, they packed it into metal boxes and milk cans and buried it under a school building. One of the young helpers left a note in with the papers. The gist of what he wrote: what we could not cry out to the world, we have buried in the ground. Part of the archive was dug up after the war. Part has never been found. Ringelblum himself did not survive. The Tanakh itself cares about writing things down, so that they can be read later by people who were not there. Job, in his suffering, cries out: "Oh that my words were now written!" Not saved. Not explained. Just written, so that someone will know. That was the quiet resistance of Oneg Shabbat. They could not stop what was happening. They could make sure it could not be denied.
screen: `A HISTORIAN AND A SECRET TEAM.` · `ONEG SHABBAT: THE JOY OF THE SABBATH.` · `BURIED IN BOXES AND MILK CANS.` · `PART FOUND, PART STILL LOST.` · then, large: `OH THAT MY WORDS WERE NOW WRITTEN.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: keep one honest record. Sit comfortably, and let your breath slow. Look back over the last day. Let one true thing rise: something you saw, something someone said, something you did that you'd rather not have, something kind that nobody noticed. Don't polish it. Just find it, and hold it in plain words. When the bell rings, write it down, on paper or in your phone, as it was. Keep it somewhere you could find it again. The bell holds the time.
They wrote it down. Emanuel Ringelblum's secret archive, Oneg Shabbat, recorded the Warsaw ghetto from inside and buried it in boxes and milk cans. Today's word.
Your line: they wrote it down. Today, write one honest sentence about something that happened, and keep it. Day one thousand twelve.

1013.title: Janusz Korczak
1013.hook: a doctor and teacher who went with his orphans to Treblinka
1013.howItsDone: Korczak's story is read in Jewish schools and at Holocaust memorial gatherings, and his ideas about respecting children are still taught to teachers and caregivers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your line was they wrote it down. Did you write one honest sentence and keep it? Today, one person from inside those same Warsaw walls, a man whose own writing survived him. Go gently. Day one thousand thirteen.

An orphanage where the children run a court. Any child can bring a complaint, even against a teacher, even against the director. The judges are children too. The house has its own newspaper and its own parliament, and a belief that a child's sorrow is never small just because the child is. The director is a doctor with a gray beard, who also writes stories for children and talks to them on the radio. He thinks children are already people, not people-in-waiting. Today's word is his name.
screen: `A COURT RUN BY CHILDREN.` → `A NEWSPAPER, A PARLIAMENT.` → `CHILDREN ARE ALREADY PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Janusz Korczak was a pen name. He was born Henryk Goldszmit, a Polish Jew, and he became a pediatrician, a writer of children's books, and the director of an orphanage for Jewish children in Warsaw. His whole life argued one thing: that children deserve respect now, not later. When the ghetto was sealed, the orphanage was forced inside the walls. Korczak went with it. He went out each day to beg for food, for medicine, for coal, for anything that would keep his children alive. At night he kept a diary, which survived. Then the deportations came. The story, as witnesses remembered it, is that when the Germans came for the orphans, Korczak would not leave them. He and his staff, among them his colleague Stefania Wilczynska, walked with the children through the streets to the trains, in rows, some say carrying a flag. The story is also told that he was offered a way to save himself, and refused. They were taken to Treblinka, and none of them came back. The psalm calls God by a tender name: "A father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows." That is how God is described, as the one who stands beside those who have no one. Korczak is not remembered for working wonders. He was a tired doctor with a diary and a house full of children. But at the end, when he could not protect them, he would not let them go alone. The orphans were his. He stayed with them.
screen: `A PEN NAME, A DOCTOR, AN ORPHANAGE.` · `BEGGING FOR FOOD IN THE GHETTO.` · `WALKING WITH THE CHILDREN.` · `HE WOULD NOT LET THEM GO ALONE.` · then, large: `A FATHER OF THE FATHERLESS.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: be with someone vulnerable. Sit, and let your breath settle. Bring to mind someone who depends on others right now: a child, a parent growing frail, a friend who is sick, a neighbor living alone. Let their face come clearly. Let one small way of being with them take shape: a visit, a call, sitting beside them, listening to the end of a long story. Hold it until the bell, and if you can, make it happen today. The bell holds the time.
Janusz Korczak. The doctor and teacher who ran a Warsaw orphanage like a children's republic, and who walked with his orphans to the trains. Today's word.
Your line: he stayed with them. Today, stay a little longer with someone who needs you, past the point where you would usually leave. Day one thousand thirteen.

1014.title: Six million
1014.hook: six million Jews were murdered, alongside Roma, disabled people and many others
1014.howItsDone: On Yom HaShoah, Israel stops for a siren while people stand in silence, and Jewish communities elsewhere hold memorial services with candles, the reading of names and the memorial prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Janusz Korczak, and your line: he stayed with them. Did you stay a little longer with someone who needed you? Today is a number, the one in the title. We'll take it slowly. Day one thousand fourteen.

A highway in Israel, mid-morning, traffic moving fast. Then a siren starts, long and steady, across the whole country at once. The cars slow and stop, right there in the lanes. Drivers open their doors and step out and stand beside them, heads down. On sidewalks, in shops, in classrooms, people stand still. Nobody speaks. Then the siren fades, and the cars start again. It's Yom HaShoah, the day of remembrance for the Holocaust. Today's word is the number they're standing for.
screen: `A SIREN ACROSS A COUNTRY.` → `DRIVERS STANDING IN THE LANES.` → `NOBODY SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Six million. That is the number of Jews murdered in the Holocaust, as Yad Vashem and historians of the Shoah count them. Men and women, grandparents, babies. Whole families, whole towns, whole ways of life. They were shot at the edges of pits, starved in ghettos, and murdered in camps built to kill. And they were not alone. The Nazis and their collaborators also murdered Roma and Sinti, disabled people, Polish civilians, Soviet prisoners of war, gay men, political prisoners and many others. Remembering one group of the dead never erases another. A number that large is almost impossible to hold. The mind slides off it. Jewish tradition has a way of turning it around. The Mishnah, in a passage about witnesses in a court where a life is at stake, teaches that one human being was created first, alone, so that we would learn this: whoever destroys a single soul is as if they destroyed a whole world, and whoever saves a single soul is as if they saved a whole world. So the title is not one number. It is six million worlds, each one complete. And what do you say in front of that? The Torah tells of Aaron, whose two sons died suddenly in the sanctuary. Moses speaks to him. And Aaron answers with nothing. "And Aaron held his peace." Some readers hear that silence not as an absence of words, but as the only honest answer. Silence is part of how the Holocaust is remembered too, as on that highway when the siren sounds.
screen: `THE JEWISH DEAD OF THE SHOAH.` · `ROMA, DISABLED PEOPLE, AND MANY OTHERS.` · `ONE SOUL, A WHOLE WORLD.` · `AARON'S SILENCE.` · then, large: `AND AARON HELD HIS PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: keep one minute of silence, and then a little more. If you can, stand, the way the drivers stand beside their cars. If you'd rather sit, sit. Let your breath slow. Don't try to picture six million. You can't, and you don't have to. Let just one person be in the silence with you, anyone, a child, an old woman, a face from an old photo. One whole world. Then let the silence hold all the others. No words. If you pray, let the silence be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Six million. The Jews murdered in the Holocaust, each one, as the Mishnah teaches, a whole world, remembered alongside the Roma, disabled people and all the others the Nazis killed. Today's word.
Your line: six million. Today, when you meet one person, let them be a whole world for a moment, the way the Mishnah asks. Day one thousand fourteen.

1015.title: Spiritual resistance
1015.hook: secret prayers, hidden schools, Shabbat kept in impossible places
1015.howItsDone: Holocaust memorials and Jewish schools teach spiritual resistance through the diaries, prayer books, drawings and ritual objects that survived from the ghettos and camps.

segments.voice: Yesterday, six million, and the silence that holds it. Did you let one person be a whole world for a moment? Today, what people kept alive inside the walls and the barracks. Day one thousand fifteen.

Friday night, in a barracks. No table, no white cloth, no wine. Bunks stacked to the ceiling, and everyone exhausted from the day's forced labor. Someone has saved a scrap of bread. Someone else knows the words by heart. In a low voice, almost a whisper, a few people begin to sing the old Shabbat melodies. Others listen from their bunks. Nothing outside has changed. But for a few minutes, inside that room, it is Shabbat. Today's word is what survivors and historians call moments like this.
screen: `FRIDAY NIGHT IN A BARRACKS.` → `A SCRAP OF BREAD, WORDS BY HEART.` → `FOR A FEW MINUTES, SHABBAT.`

segments.voice: Spiritual resistance means refusing to let the enemy decide who you are, even when you cannot stop what they do to you. In the ghettos and the camps, survivors describe it in many forms. Where Jewish schooling was forbidden, teachers held classes in secret, with lookouts at the door and books hidden under coats. People prayed in hiding, sometimes from memory, because the prayer books were gone. Survivors tell of Shabbat candles made from scraps, of tefillin smuggled from hand to hand, of a Passover seder held with no matzah, only the story. There were secret libraries, choirs, lectures and poems. And there were people who could not pray, or chose not to, who kept their dignity in other ways: sharing bread, telling jokes, writing down the truth. Each of these was a way of saying: you have not made us into what you say we are. In the Warsaw ghetto, a rabbi named Yitzhak Nissenbaum is remembered for a teaching about this. In earlier times of persecution, he said, Jews were asked to sanctify God's name by dying, if they had to, rather than give up their faith. But now the enemy wanted Jewish lives themselves. So the holy task was kiddush ha-chayim, the sanctification of life: to stay alive, and stay human, as an act of faith. The Torah gives one command that turns time itself into something holy. "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." No building is needed. No candles, even, if there are none. A day can still be set apart by people who remember it. In impossible places, some of them did.
screen: `REFUSING TO BE WHAT THEY SAY.` · `SECRET CLASSES, PRAYERS BY HEART.` · `THE SANCTIFICATION OF LIFE.` · `A DAY SET APART BY MEMORY.` · then, large: `REMEMBER THE SABBATH DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: keep one practice today. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind one small thing you do that keeps you yourself: lighting candles, a blessing before eating, reading a page, a walk, a song, calling your mother. It may be religious or not. Hold it, and notice how easily it could slip today, and how much it would mean to keep it on purpose. Decide when you'll do it. If you pray, this sit can be your prayer. If you don't, let it be a promise to yourself. The bell holds the time.
Spiritual resistance. Secret prayers, hidden classes, Shabbat kept in barracks: refusing to let the enemy decide who you are. Today's word.

Your line: they kept shabbat. Today, keep one practice of yours on purpose, however small. This week ran from the children on the trains, through closed doors, the ghettos, the buried archive, Korczak and the six million, to this. Day one thousand fifteen.
